context_blurb:
Stand in the sunshine one morning and look at your shadow. Look again at lunchtime, and once more late in the afternoon. It will have shrunk, then stretched, and swung around to point a new way. The Sun seems to cross the sky, but the real traveller is the ground under your feet. Earth is spinning, and its spin makes day, night and the changing shadows.

Earth spins like a top. It turns around its axis, an imaginary line that passes straight through the middle of the planet, with the North Pole at one end and the South Pole at the other. Earth never stops turning, and one full spin takes about 24 hours. That one spin is a day. Earth also travels around the Sun, along a path called its orbit, but one trip around takes a whole year.

As Earth turns, it carries each town into the Sun's light and then around into darkness, again and again. At any moment, the half of Earth facing the Sun has day, and the half turned away has night. So day and night come from Earth spinning around, not from its yearly trip around the Sun. People long believed that the Sun circled a still Earth, because we cannot feel the ground move. In truth the Sun only seems to circle us.

That means two places on opposite sides of Earth have opposite times of day: when it is midday in one town, it is around midnight in the town on the exact other side, which faces away from the Sun. Half a day later, the two swap.

Because Earth spins toward the east, the Sun seems to rise in the east, climb across the sky and set in the west, so its daily path runs from east to west. It is like riding in a car: the trees outside seem to slide backward, though it is really the car that moves.

A shadow is the dark patch where something blocks the light. A shadow always falls on the side of an object away from the Sun. So if your shadow stretches out ahead of you, the Sun is at your back, and you are facing away from it.

As the Sun seems to move, shadows swing around. In the morning the Sun is in the eastern sky, so a stick's shadow points roughly west. By late afternoon the Sun has moved over to the western sky, and the same shadow has swung around to point roughly toward the east. A sundial tells the time by this swing, and people in ancient Egypt were telling time with stick shadows some 3,500 years ago.

Shadows change length too. The lower the Sun sits, the more its light comes in at a slant, and the longer the shadows it casts. So when a tree's shadow reaches far across a field, many times the tree's own height, the Sun must be low in the sky, near sunrise or sunset. A high Sun makes short shadows, and only a Sun directly overhead would leave a tree's shade lying right beneath it.

You can see the pattern for yourself: mark the tip of a pole's shadow once an hour, from morning till evening. The shadow starts out long just after sunrise, shrinks to its shortest around midday, when the Sun is highest, and grows long again toward sunset: long, then short, then long again. Far from the equator even the noon shadow never quite vanishes, because there the Sun never climbs directly overhead.
